The Composed
Wordmark

Every poster was being offered the same handful of wordmark treatments, because choosing one was cheaper than inventing one. This round changed the price. Three posters, three treatments, and none of them off a list.

Reviewed by the band

The band has now seen this work. Reported 2026‑08‑30: every member read the shared material and looked at the artwork. They like the wordmark, the skull, the year rings and the timeline, and they love the illustrated generated work.

That is a response to a direction, not a signature on each item. Individual artefacts, whether Böbbis becomes a standing per-release character, whether the skull is ever publicly named, and printing or selling anything are all still open. Where a direction was chosen inside a round, that was Marcus’s call.

Start with the plain-language overview if you haven’t already.

1

Where this sits

Every illustrated poster ends the same way: the real APEZONE wordmark laid across the top of the picture. The letterforms never change — they always come from the shipped master file. What changes is the colour and the surface treatment.

The previous round fixed the rule that decided whether a treatment was legible. This round is about where the treatment comes from — and it ends with the eight built-in treatments demoted from a menu to a set of worked examples.

One picture was regenerated, at a cost of 150 credits. Everything else here is deterministic.

2

Not artwork

All three posters on this page are concepts. Nothing is printed, nothing is on merchandise, and the shipped logo itself is untouched by any of it. Open decision 12 — the generation licence — still blocks print and merch.

The band has seen and liked the illustrated direction. It has not reviewed these three pictures, or these wordmark treatments.

3

The complaint: the options were always the same

Marcus, looking at a set of wordmark options: “Did we give the possibility to create custom options for each poster? As now it kind of seems that in every poster the options are the same…” And then the point underneath it:

Marcus, 2026-08-31

“Because I rather have it made into a creative process instead. Not a generic one. I don’t want every wordmark to look like the same.”

4

Why a menu wins even when a better route exists

The awkward part: the better route already existed and nobody used it. A day earlier the pipeline had learned to accept a treatment written specifically for one poster, rather than only names from its built-in list. Two posters used it. Nothing else changed.

The reason is not taste and not discipline. It is cost:

Writing a new treatment cost about forty lines. Picking one off the list cost nothing. So the list won every single time, including when the person reaching for it knew better. A capability that is more expensive than the thing it replaces does not get used.

Which makes the fix structural rather than a matter of trying harder: make inventing one cheaper than choosing one.

5

The kit: a vocabulary, not a longer list

The tempting mistake was to add the good improvisations to the eight. That produces a menu of twelve and the same problem.

Instead there is now a small vocabulary of parts — a flat fill, a grown keyline, a stroke-only ring, a horizontal band, repeating strips, an offset ghost copy, a trailing extrude block, a vertical gradient, a soft halo — which get stacked. A whole treatment is one to four lines:

TREATMENT = K.stack(K.split(-9, 5, "#DC7F41"),   # the warm plate, slipped left
                    K.split(9, -5, "#1A7982"),   # the teal plate, slipped right
                    K.keyline(4),
                    K.fill("face"))

That is a two-colour printing misregistration, and it exists for exactly one poster. Three rules survive the change unaltered:

  • The letterforms are never redrawn. Every part repaints the shipped master's own outline. That is what makes invention safe.
  • The gate still vetoes. A composed treatment is measured against the real artwork exactly like a built-in one.
  • Scripted yes, generated no. Asking an image model for a wordmark treatment was tested a fortnight ago: ten candidates, and all ten came back a different word.
6

Composed for Senate Square

Marcus asked for something futuristic, the theme being a UFO attack. Five compositions, each reasoned from what is actually in this picture rather than from a list:

The chosen one measures 17.28 — the highest separation of any mark tried on any poster across both rounds — and the ring keeps the night sky reading through the letterforms. The idea is the picture's own: everything else in the beam is being lifted, so the band name is too.

7

Composed for Kauppatori — where the best score was the wrong answer

Marcus: “Let's try the mis-register on Kauppatori too.” Which is the real test of the idea, because it must not be the same misregistration. This scene prints in two families — a warm orange at 20% of its coloured pixels, a teal at 14% — so those are the two plates that slip.

The control scored highest and is plainly wrong. Senate Square's magenta and cyan measure 5.05 here, the best of the six — and they look imported, because neither ink appears anywhere in this picture.

The measurement asks whether a mark separates from the artwork. It has no way of asking whether the colours belong to it. Choosing by the number would have put one poster's palette on another poster.

The version taken is the genuine two-way slip in the picture's own inks, keeping the acid yellow: 4.84, against the previous treatment's 3.05.

8

Two faults found by eye, not by a gate

Both were spotted by Marcus looking at a picture, and neither was visible to any automated check.

The offset that had no colour of its own. “This type is a bit boring if the offset is the same color as the main fill.” He was looking at a real regression introduced the previous day. The older colour code always brightened its chosen colour to make the letter face, so any treatment using the unbrightened version as its shadow got separation for free. The replacement picks a colour that is often already bright enough, skips the brightening — and the two roles become the same colour.

And a dot screen that printed white specks. The regenerated Senate Square source measures smooth, which for the first time ever triggered the pipeline's add-a-halftone path on a poster. It went wrong immediately:

Abandoned after three attempts, and the reason is a limit rather than a setting. Marcus asked whether this meant no dots at all any more. Worth checking, and the check unwound the whole approach.

First, the scope was smaller than it sounded: only this one poster ever used the add-a-screen path. The other two carry halftone drawn in by the generator.

Then three fixes, each better, none sufficient. The repair written down first — take the paper colour from a percentile rather than the brightest pixel — does not work: the screened area is a single flat colour, so every percentile of it is that same colour and the dots vanish entirely. Deriving the gaps as a shadow of the flat did give ink-coloured dots. Dropping the luminance window then moved them off the lit hull, where they read as dirt, into the shadowed planes, where they read as grain. Marcus stopped the fourth attempt, with six reference posters where the halftone works:

Marcus, 2026-08-31

“It’s more meaningful if it is a certain element in the image. Not just applied to a certain hue with a certain strength.” And of one reference: “I would have left it out of the lightning strikes.”

That cannot be expressed from here. The code selects a quantised colour, so the screen lands on every region sharing it — on this poster the saucer hull, patches of night sky and parts of the crowd at once. A reduction to the single largest contiguous region was half-written and thrown away: it would have tidied the scatter and still could not say the sky but not the lightning in it, because the lightning is a different element in the same zone, often in the same hue. A colour-plus-threshold mask has no notion of an element, and giving it one means image segmentation.

The rule was already written down — halftone after the fact is a treatment inside artwork already drawn in the right register, never a converter into it — and this project's own three posters are the evidence:

PosterHalftoneWhere it came fromReads
Kauppatori0.053drawn by the generatorcorrectly
Worship0.044drawn by the generatorcorrectly
Senate Square0.028post-appliedout of place

So the screen is off, and the fix is to ask for the halftone in the prompt next time this scene is regenerated. A source that wants dots wants them in its prompt. What survives, because it is honest and changes no default: a shadow-derived sheet, and the ability to aim a screen at a chosen luminance band.

Done, 2026-08-31 — and it revealed a fault in the measurement above. The scene was regenerated with the dots written into its style block and they arrived: a real screen through the night sky and the shaded hull, with the beam and the neon left solid. It still measures 0.033. The number in this table averages the whole frame, so a screen correctly confined to the flats cannot reach the threshold — least of all in a near-black sky. The next round has the evidence.

9

The wheelchair

The band's singer asked for a man to be carried up the tractor beam still sitting in his wheelchair. The picture was regenerated with that written into the brief — played deadpan, exactly as seriously as everything else in the frame.

One thing on the record about Böbbis’s head. Marcus looked at the new face and said it was fine, which is consistent — the previously approved version of this poster has the same head, and that was checked rather than assumed.

But the written character description asks for a narrow lower jaw and no cranium, and these pictures have neither. So the description and the posters disagree, and it is the description that is out of step. Reconciling the text is open work; nothing was quietly changed to hide the gap.

Settled 2026-08-31, and this paragraph was half wrong. Checked at full size, the jaw is there and it is the narrow one the character round chose; so are the cheek arches and the heart-shaped nose. Only the clause about the back of the skull diverged, and it was a claim a face-on drawing could never have tested. The description was corrected; nothing was regenerated. The next round has the comparison.

It is recorded in the decisions log: a fourth poster should be neither a ring nor a slip.

11

What this concluded

  • A capability nobody uses is not a capability. Per-poster treatments were possible for a day and stayed unused, because choosing was cheaper than composing. Changing the cost changed the behaviour; asking for more discipline would not have.
  • The eight built-in treatments are examples now, not options. They still work and one still ships.
  • A colour must belong to its own picture. Borrowing another poster's inks measures fine and looks imported, and no gate here can tell the difference.
  • Both faults this round were found by a person looking at a picture. Neither the separation gate nor the two older gates could see either of them.

One statement made during the round was simply wrong and is corrected here: while measuring Kauppatori's inks it was claimed that the teal sky fell below the threshold for being counted as a colour, and so never reached the scorer. It did not — the teal was present the whole time, at 18% and 14%. A score-sorted list was misread as an all-warm one.

13

Method, and what this cannot show

  • No band review of any picture or any treatment on this page.
  • Nothing was seen on paper. Screen only. No print proof, and no check of how any of it survives a streaming platform's cover-art compression.
  • Thumbnail behaviour was checked by eye at 64 pixels, and it decided things — a thin ring is legible on a poster and gone on a phone, which is why the rings here are thick. It is automated as of 2026-08-31, and its first act was to fail the worship poster on this page — the next round.
  • The separation measurement is calibrated to one observer — fifty test images judged by Claude, not by a person. That caveat carries over from the previous round and is the largest one on either page.
  • The dot-screen fault is patched per poster, not repaired. §8 — and the replacement route was taken the same day, which found a fault in the measurement itself.
  • The character description disagreed with the pictures — §9, settled 2026-08-31, and in one clause rather than the several claimed here.
  • Two image generations, 150 credits. Everything else is deterministic and re-runnable from the poster files.
